The cells are predominantly polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Very high counts above 25,000/mm³ can occasionally occur with very active disease but require evaluation for infection. 
Synovial fluid complement levels may be reduced despite elevated serum complement levels. Thus, the patient's inflammatory neutrophil-predominant fluid is compatible with rheumatoid arthritis. Clinical context is essential when evaluating an acutely inflamed joint because septic arthritis must still be excluded when appropriate.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman has 4 months of inflammatory hand pain and swelling. Plain radiographs show no erosions, but clinical examination strongly suggests rheumatoid arthritis. Which imaging modality is particularly useful for detecting early joint abnormalities before radiographic bone erosions become apparent?
questions.explanation:
MRI and ultrasonography are useful in early rheumatoid arthritis before conventional radiographs demonstrate erosive changes. MRI can demonstrate synovial thickening and bone marrow edema. Bone marrow edema may appear as decreased signal on T1-weighted sequences and increased enhancement after gadolinium. Synovial thickening on MRI has also been shown to predict future bony erosions. 
Conventional radiographs are more useful for demonstrating established changes such as periarticular osteopenia, joint-space narrowing, and marginal erosions.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and has active inflammatory polyarthritis. She has never received a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug. Which treatment is recommended as initial therapy?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate is identified in the source as the initial drug of choice for rheumatoid arthritis. Early initiation of DMARD therapy is emphasized because treatment aims to prevent irreversible joint damage and disability. In patients with early disease and low disease activity, methotrexate monotherapy is specifically preferred. Leflunomide or sulfasalazine can be used when methotrexate is contraindicated or not tolerated. TNF inhibitors and other biologic agents are generally considered after inadequate response to conventional DMARD therapy.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is taking a biologic DMARD. She develops fever, productive cough, hypotension, and positive blood cultures consistent with a serious bacterial infection. What is the most appropriate approach to her rheumatoid arthritis medication?
options: Temporarily hold the biologic until the infection resolves
Immediately switch to another biologic agent
questions.explanation: Biologic and targeted synthetic DMARDs increase the risk of serious infections. It is  recommended holding these agents during an active serious infection. Therapy can be resumed after the infection has resolved and antimicrobial treatment has been completed. Patients receiving these medications should also be assessed for opportunistic infections, including tuberculosis and fungal infections. Live vaccines should be avoided while receiving biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD therapy.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man from a Bangladesh presents with gradually worsening mid-back pain for 5 months. He has lost 5 kg during this period and recently developed weakness in both lower limbs. Temperature is 37.2°C, and examination reveals mild thoracic kyphosis. A chest radiograph shows no pulmonary lesions. MRI demonstrates destruction of adjacent thoracic vertebral bodies with a paraspinal fluid collection.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tuberculous spondylitis, or Pott disease, is tuberculosis involving the vertebral bodies and often the intervertebral disc. It commonly presents with chronic back pain, weakness, paraplegia, and kyphotic deformity. Constitutional symptoms such as fever and weight loss may occur but are often less pronounced than in pyogenic spinal infection. Large paraspinal abscesses with relatively mild inflammatory findings are particularly characteristic of spinal TB. The disease commonly affects the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine. A normal chest radiograph does not exclude spinal TB because pulmonary lesions may be clinically silent or absent on imaging.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with chronic back pain undergoes MRI with gadolinium administration. Which MRI pattern is most consistent with tuberculous spondylitis?
options: T1 hyperintensity and T2 hyperintensity without enhancement
T1 hypointensity and T2 hypointensity with no enhancement
questions.explanation: Tuberculous spondylitis causes inflammatory changes within the vertebral marrow. On MRI, affected marrow is typically hypointense on T1-weighted sequences. It is generally hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences because of increased water content and inflammatory tissue. Gadolinium-enhanced imaging demonstrates enhancement of marrow, subligamentous tissue, discal tissue, and sometimes the dura. MRI is particularly useful for identifying epidural disease and spinal cord compression. These findings help distinguish active spinal infection from several noninfectious causes of vertebral destruction.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man presents with slowly progressive back pain and a large paravertebral mass. Despite the impressive size of the lesion, he has only mild tenderness, no high fever, and minimal surrounding inflammatory changes. Imaging shows a well-circumscribed fluid collection with an enhancing wall.
Which term best describes this lesion?
questions.explanation: A large paraspinal abscess associated with tuberculosis is classically called a cold abscess. It may develop gradually and produce surprisingly little pain or systemic inflammation. Unlike many pyogenic abscesses, it may lack frank pus and prominent inflammatory signs. On imaging, these collections are often large and well circumscribed, with a fluid center and a relatively well-defined enhancing margin. Cold abscess formation is a classic feature of late-stage spinal tuberculosis. Recognition of this pattern should increase suspicion for a granulomatous infection such as TB.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old child with spinal tuberculosis is being evaluated for deformity. The intervertebral disc is involved relatively early compared with an adult patient with the same disease.
Which factor best explains this difference?
options: Children have greater vertebral bone density
Children have stronger anterior longitudinal ligaments
Children have a richer blood supply to the intervertebral disc
questions.explanation: The intervertebral disc is relatively avascular, particularly in adults. This contributes to its relative preservation in adult tuberculous spondylitis. In children, however, the disc has a considerably richer blood supply. Consequently, disc involvement can occur earlier in children with spinal TB. Despite this, disc involvement is still generally less prominent than in pyogenic spinal infection.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman has chronic thoracolumbar pain and mild bilateral leg weakness. MRI reveals vertebral destruction, a large paraspinal abscess, and extension into the epidural space. The physician wants the most sensitive imaging study to determine whether the spinal cord is compressed.
Which is the best next study?
questions.explanation: MRI is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating spinal tuberculosis when epidural involvement or cord compression is suspected. It provides excellent visualization of the vertebral marrow, intervertebral disc, paraspinal collections, epidural soft tissue, and spinal cord. CT can demonstrate bony destruction well, but it is inferior to MRI for assessing neural structures. Plain radiographs may miss early disease because vertebral and disc abnormalities can initially be subtle. Contrast-enhanced MRI can also show enhancement of marrow, subligamentous tissue, dura, and epidural inflammatory tissue. This makes MRI particularly important in patients with neurological symptoms.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old man from a tuberculosis-endemic region has back pain. Radiographs show erosion of adjacent vertebral bodies, but the intervertebral disc space remains relatively preserved. MRI demonstrates vertebral erosion with an apparently preserved disc.
Which radiologic sign is this finding most consistent with?
questions.explanation: The floating disc sign refers to relative preservation of the intervertebral disc despite adjacent vertebral destruction. It is particularly recognized in adults with tuberculous spondylitis. The disc tends to be relatively spared because of its poor vascularity. This contrasts with pyogenic spondylitis, in which disc destruction is often more prominent. Although the disc can eventually become involved, early preservation is a useful clue to spinal TB. The finding should be interpreted together with other features such as subligamentous spread, paraspinal abscesses, and vertebral destruction.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is being treated for confirmed tuberculous spondylitis. After several months of appropriate treatment, his back pain and inflammatory markers have improved. MRI still shows persistent enhancement around the previously affected vertebrae.
Which is the best interpretation?
options: Enhancement may persist despite clinical and laboratory improvement
Persistent enhancement proves development of a pyogenic superinfection
Enhancement should disappear within 1 week of therapy
Persistent MRI enhancement always indicates treatment failure
questions.explanation: MRI abnormalities may lag behind clinical recovery in spinal tuberculosis. Reduction in enhancement can begin within weeks to months after treatment starts. However, enhancement can persist for a prolonged period, sometimes up to 12 months. Therefore, persistent enhancement alone does not necessarily indicate active or failed treatment. Clinical status and laboratory improvement should be considered alongside imaging findings. Plain radiographic evidence of healing can also take many months, sometimes up to approximately 15 months.

questions.question: A 21-year-old male football player falls and experiences sudden severe shoulder pain and a sensation that the shoulder has "popped out." Examination suggests an anterior shoulder dislocation. Which mechanism most likely produced this injury?
options: Anteriorly directed force with the arm abducted and externally rotated
Inferiorly directed force with the arm internally rotated
Posteriorly directed force with the arm adducted
Axial compression with the arm flexed
questions.explanation: Traumatic anterior shoulder instability typically results from an anteriorly directed force applied while the shoulder is abducted and externally rotated. This position places substantial stress on the anterior stabilizing structures of the glenohumeral joint. The injury may result in an anterior dislocation and subsequent recurrent instability. The anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament is particularly important in this position. The injury pattern may include labral damage and a Hill-Sachs lesion. Therefore, the combination of abduction, external rotation, and an anterior force is the classic mechanism.

questions.question: A competitive rugby player sustains his first traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. After reduction, he is counseled about the risk of future instability. Which factor in this patient most strongly increases the likelihood of recurrence?
options: Participation in a noncontact recreational sport
questions.explanation: Young age is a major risk factor for recurrent anterior shoulder instability. The recurrence rates can be as high as 80–90% in teenagers, with approximately a 90% chance of recurrence in patients younger than 20 years. Contact athletes also have an increased incidence of instability. Military populations are similarly considered high-risk. This high recurrence risk is one reason surgery may be considered after even a first dislocation in selected young athletes.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man has recurrent episodes of his shoulder "giving way." During examination, the arm is placed at 90° of abduction and 90° of external rotation. The patient becomes apprehensive and resists further positioning. Which physical examination maneuver has been performed?
questions.explanation: The apprehension test is performed with the patient's shoulder at 90° of abduction and 90° of external rotation. A positive test occurs when the patient experiences apprehension in this position. The maneuver is designed to reproduce the position associated with anterior instability. The relocation test differs because an anteriorly directed force is then applied to the shoulder to decrease apprehension. The sulcus sign is assessed with the arm at the patient's side and evaluates inferior laxity. Therefore, the described examination is the classic apprehension test.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man with recurrent anterior shoulder instability develops marked apprehension during the apprehension test. The examiner then applies an anteriorly directed force to the shoulder, and the patient's apprehension decreases dramatically. Which test is positive?
questions.explanation: The relocation sign is present when apprehension decreases after an anteriorly directed force is applied to the shoulder during apprehension testing. This finding supports the diagnosis of anterior shoulder instability. The initial apprehension test is performed with the arm at 90° of abduction and external rotation. In contrast, the sulcus sign is performed with the arm at the side and assesses inferior laxity. Generalized ligamentous laxity is evaluated using the Beighton criteria, with a score greater than 4 indicating hyperlaxity in the provided material.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man presents with several years of recurrent, well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by thick, silvery-white scales. The lesions are most prominent over both elbows and knees and have recently appeared on the scalp. He reports that the lesions improve during summer and worsen during winter. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Plaque psoriasis is the most common form of psoriasis and accounts for approximately 85–90% of cases. It characteristically produces sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales. The extensor surfaces, especially the elbows and knees, as well as the scalp and lumbosacral region, are typical sites. Psoriasis is chronic and follows a relapsing-remitting course rather than resolving permanently. The provided material notes that sunlight and summer conditions generally improve psoriasis, whereas winter tends to aggravate it. Seborrheic dermatitis more commonly affects sebaceous areas and usually lacks the classic thick silvery scale described here.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman with known psoriasis develops several new psoriatic plaques exactly along the linear distribution of scratches she received from a cat 2 weeks earlier. Which of the following best explains this finding?
questions.explanation: The Koebner phenomenon refers to the development of psoriatic lesions at sites of skin trauma. Mechanical, chemical, or radiation-induced injury can trigger lesions in susceptible patients. It is considered an indicator of active psoriasis in the provided material. This phenomenon is distinct from the Auspitz sign, which is pinpoint bleeding seen after removal of psoriatic scales. Dactylitis refers to sausage-shaped swelling of an entire finger or toe and is associated with psoriatic arthritis.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy develops numerous small, erythematous, scaly, raindrop-shaped lesions over his trunk and back several weeks after recovering from a sore throat. Which subtype of psoriasis is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Guttate psoriasis is characterized by numerous small, raindrop-shaped erythematous and scaly lesions. It commonly occurs in children or young patients after an upper respiratory tract infection caused by streptococcal organisms. The lesions predominantly involve the trunk and back. It differs from plaque psoriasis, which produces larger, well-demarcated plaques, often on extensor surfaces. According to the source, guttate psoriasis has the best prognosis among the psoriasis subtypes described. Recognition of the preceding streptococcal infection and the distinctive morphology is particularly useful for diagnosis.

questions.question: A dermatologist gently removes the scales from a psoriatic plaque on a patient's knee. Multiple pinpoint bleeding spots become visible beneath the removed scale. Which clinical sign has been demonstrated?
questions.explanation: The Auspitz sign is characterised by pinpoint bleeding after successive removal of psoriatic scales. It is a useful clinical sign supporting the diagnosis of psoriasis. The finding results from the characteristic changes in the epidermis and superficial dermal vasculature associated with psoriatic plaques. Koebner phenomenon, in contrast, refers to the development of new lesions at sites of trauma. Nikolsky sign is associated with disorders such as pemphigus and involves epidermal shearing with pressure.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman has a skin biopsy performed because the appearance of her plaques is atypical. Histologic examination shows epidermal hyperplasia, parakeratosis, elongated rete ridges, dilated and tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae, and spongiform pustules. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
questions.explanation: Psoriasis has characteristic histopathologic findings that reflect accelerated and abnormal epidermal turnover. These include parakeratosis, epidermal hyperplasia, regular elongation of the rete ridges, and dilated and tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae. Spongiform pustules of Kogoj are another characteristic finding described in the source. The biopsy may also demonstrate an absence of the granular layer. Histopathology is not routinely necessary when the clinical presentation is classic, but it can help distinguish psoriasis from other dermatoses when the diagnosis is uncertain.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis develops painful swelling of several fingers. On examination, an entire finger is swollen in a uniform, sausage-like fashion. He also reports lower back pain. Which of the following is the most likely associated condition?
questions.explanation: Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis and occurs in approximately 30% of patients according to the source. It commonly occurs alongside skin and nail disease. A characteristic manifestation is dactylitis, in which an entire finger or toe becomes diffusely swollen, producing a sausage-like appearance. Psoriatic arthritis can also involve the spine and sacroiliac joints, causing spondylitis and sacroiliitis. This combination of psoriasis, dactylitis, and axial symptoms strongly suggests psoriatic arthritis. It is clinically important because it can have a major negative effect on functional prognosis.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with stable plaque psoriasis develops a significant flare shortly after starting a new medication. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Several medications are identified in the provided material as potential aggravating factors for psoriasis. These include chloroquine, lithium, beta-blockers, steroids, and NSAIDs. Thus, a newly introduced beta-blocker can plausibly explain worsening of previously stable disease. The source also identifies infections, psychological stress, alcohol, smoking, obesity, hypocalcemia, and trauma as possible triggers. Recognizing medication-related exacerbations is important because modifying an aggravating factor may help improve disease control. The other listed medications are not specifically identified as psoriasis triggers in the provided text.
